overview: The atlas assigns “Tungusic Tribes” to a 1200 to 1279 polygon, but neither word proves a single people, state, self-name, language, or border. The decoded shape covers parts of the Olekma and Aldan basins, the Dzhugdzhur interior, and a narrow reach toward the lower Amur. It includes Olekminsk, Aldan, Ust-Maya, and Nelkan probes, while excluding Yakutsk, Okhotsk, Chita, and Khabarovsk. Scholarship distinguishes later documented Evenki, Even, Negidal, and neighboring histories, while early movements and language distributions remain debated. Even a proposed thirteenth-century “Small Houses” culture is known from only four settlements and has been reinterpreted using later evidence. This card teaches what the atlas draws and what evidence supports. Later ethnography can illuminate possible skills such as portable housing, fishing, hunting, reindeer care, plant knowledge, companionship, and learning, but it cannot become a diary of 1200. No securely localized exact-period Tungusic writing survives inside the polygon. In 1279 the atlas repaints most probes “Siberians” and one “Yuan,” a software seam rather than a mass identity change.

periods.title: 1200 to 1210: an atlas umbrella appears
periods.summary: The sole target polygon appears in the 1200 snapshot beside Mongol Empire and Paleo-Siberian hunter-gatherer features. A 1207 campaign reached forest peoples around Oirat and Yenisei regions far west of most target probes. Neither event creates one Tungusic polity across the drawn shape.

periods.title: 1210 to 1220: forest people remains an outsider category
periods.summary: Mongol-era writing grouped varied northern communities as forest people. Researchers disagree about the campaign's precise reach and participants. That category should not be translated into Tungusic Tribes, projected over the polygon, or treated as proof that Olekma, Aldan, Dzhugdzhur, and lower Amur communities shared one government.

periods.title: 1220 to 1230: names and sites remain uneven
periods.summary: The Secret History records Jochi's expedition, but its named peoples and route do not securely identify this entire eastern polygon. Archaeological labels also have their own locations and dates. A source can be exact-period yet still be geographically unable to narrate every household colored by the atlas.

periods.title: 1230 to 1240: language history stays a hypothesis
periods.summary: Modern linguistic work distinguishes northern Tungusic languages and reconstructs earlier movements, yet the first detailed distributions come from much later records. Pots, camps, and hunting grounds do not announce their speakers. The atlas label remains a retrospective research guess, not a recovered thirteenth-century census category.

periods.title: 1240 to 1250: household evidence has limits
periods.summary: A proposed thirteenth-century Small Houses culture once seemed relevant to medieval Yakutia, but only four settlements were known and later analysis tied its traits to fourteenth- through sixteenth-century Kulun-Atakh contexts. This dispute warns against furnishing the target with one uniform house, herd, or ethnic identity.

periods.title: 1250 to 1260: images resist exact dating
periods.summary: Rock imagery in northern Yakutia includes layers assigned broadly to several archaeological periods, while some marks may have been refreshed later. Without secure context, a medieval-looking image cannot narrate the target decade, identify a language, or prove that every community shared its meaning.

periods.title: 1260 to 1270: writing evidence stays outside
periods.summary: Jurchen is the earliest Tungusic language with native-script materials, including a securely dated 1127 inscription from Arkhara. That evidence is earlier than this interval and south of the polygon. It proves that related writing existed elsewhere, not that one umbrella text represented northern households here.

periods.title: 1270 to 1279: the map prepares a mass repaint
periods.summary: At the 1279 snapshot the exact id disappears. Eight former target probes become Siberians and Nikolaevsk becomes Yuan Dynasty; the same sampled pattern persists at 1300 and 1400. Such synchronized relabeling reflects the atlas's categories, not a documented day when communities exchanged identities.

sections.title: Read the exact map before interpreting its label

items.text: The index contains one exact tungusic-tribes record: a circa culture from 1200 to 1279, generated from historical basemaps. It has one border file, no card, no override, and no exact imported summary. Its coverage queue says Europe even though its decoded geometry lies in Asia.

The target is one polygon with one ring and 63 positions. Its bounding box runs from about 115.39 to 142.72 degrees east and 51.56 to 61.80 degrees north. That northern East Siberian footprint differs sharply from both earlier Tungus cards and cannot share their text.

Olekminsk, Neryungri, Aldan, Bomnak, Ust-Maya, the central watershed, Dzhugdzhur, Nelkan, and Nikolaevsk test inside. Yakutsk, Okhotsk, Magadan, Ayan, Chumikan, Chita, Zeya, Khabarovsk, and northern Sakhalin test outside. These probe results describe software geometry by design, not a surveyed cultural frontier.

The target shares one encoded topology arc with the Mongol Empire and one with Paleo-Siberian hunter-gatherers. Northern Sakhalin belongs to the separate Ainu feature. Shared arcs explain how the basemap tiles space; they do not prove treaties, guarded borders, ethnic edges, or medieval passport desks.

At 1200, many western and southern control probes switch from Mongols to Mongol Empire, while nine probes switch from Mongols to this target. At 1279, twenty-nine of thirty-one sampled owners change at once. Those large seams expose cartographic repainting, not synchronized conquest or migration.

sections.title: Use Tungusic as a careful linguistic umbrella

items.text: Tungusic is a modern scholarly name for a language family. It is not evidence that every person inside the polygon used one language, called themselves Tungusic, shared ancestry, or recognized a common border. Community histories and language shifts require evidence at smaller scales than this atlas supplies.

Scholars distinguish later documented Negidal, eastern Evenki, and Okhotsk Even histories around the Amur and Okhotsk worlds. Their relationships matter, but back-projecting those modern names to every thirteenth-century household would erase change. The atlas label should remain visibly retrospective and plural.

A recent contact study maps Evenki, Even, Sakha, Yukaghiric, and other languages from much later records, then discusses possible earlier movements. Its hypotheses are useful precisely because they remain hypotheses. A modern distribution map is not a transparent window onto the year 1200.

The Brill history follows coastal and river communities through shifting contacts rather than treating language as biological destiny. People can marry, trade, move, and change speech. Related languages therefore do not guarantee one economy, political loyalty, ritual system, or origin story across the target.

The atlas has separate tungus, tungus-700, and tungusic-tribes ids. Their dates, shapes, neighbors, and evidence differ. Repeated English labels reveal the basemap maker's taxonomy, not an unbroken nation marching through fifteen centuries with one name tag and extremely durable border paint.

sections.title: Keep Mongol power and forest communities geographically bounded

items.text: The Secret History says Jochi went against the People of the Forest in 1207. That phrase is an outsider political category within a court narrative, not a list of Tungusic speakers. The text must be read with its genre, later transmission, named route, and selective interests visible.

One study places the 1207 expedition chiefly toward the Oirat and Yenisei Kyrgyz, well west of the target's Aldan and Dzhugdzhur core. It directly challenges a lazy map-to-story match. A campaign somewhere in northern Asia cannot automatically conquer every northern polygon.

Another analysis links the expedition to Mongol control of the Sayano-Altai and Yenisei region. Its argument concerns imperial expansion but still does not document administration at Olekminsk, Ust-Maya, Nelkan, or Nikolaevsk. Political history must follow named places rather than convenient colors.

Research on Siberia under the Mongol Empire emphasizes that forest people covered varied communities and relationships. Tribute, alliance, submission, flight, exchange, and indirect authority could differ by place. The phrase cannot be upgraded into one ethnicity or a uniform province without local evidence.

Mongol-era sources are strongest for the peoples and places they actually name. Their silences cannot become a household survey of this polygon. Even a wonderfully detailed court narrative cannot report from every camp its author never visited, however much a modern reader wishes it had.

sections.title: Build homes, move camps, and manage cold cautiously

items.text: Later architectural research compares many Tungusic-speaking communities and finds multiple dwelling forms. That variety is the lesson to carry backward: climate, season, materials, mobility, and local history shaped homes. It does not authorize one standard thirteenth-century Tungusic tent across a polygon larger than many countries.

A study of later Evenki housing describes structures made from locally available willow, birch, and hides to handle cold, rain, snow, heat, and wind. These demonstrate skilled environmental design. They are analogies for possibilities, not excavated proof that every 1200 household used identical materials.

Portable architecture requires choosing poles and coverings, arranging a hearth, controlling smoke, drying equipment, and packing efficiently. Later ethnography shows such expertise, but exact medieval layouts remain unexcavated within this polygon. A quick-looking camp could embody years of knowledge and decidedly unquick setup decisions.

The Small Houses debate warns that even excavated buildings can be misdated or overclassified. Only four settlements supported the original category, and later finds changed its interpretation. House size and pottery traits do not automatically identify language, ethnicity, or a map-wide social system.

No reviewed excavation securely supplies a complete 1200 to 1279 target household inventory. The responsible reconstruction separates direct geometry, nearby disputed archaeology, and later ethnographic comparison. Readers get fewer imaginary sofas, but a much clearer account of what evidence can actually carry.

sections.title: Find food, work, animals, and seasonal routes

items.text: Later collaborative research records fishing, herd watching, treating reindeer, training calves, collective hunting, meat sharing, and camp construction among Evenki participants. These activities reveal linked technical and social knowledge. They cannot be assigned unchanged to 1200, but they show why “hunter” or “herder” alone is inadequate.

Modern ethnobotanical research documents food plants as nutrition, medicine, ritual practice, and cultural knowledge among Evenki communities. Gathering is skilled work involving season, place, identification, preparation, and memory. None of those modern details should be silently turned into an exact medieval menu for the whole polygon.

Ethnoarchaeology of Evenki hunting and reindeer herding shows how mobile work leaves a selective material record. Camps may be brief, reused, or cleaned; animals and equipment move. Sparse remains therefore do not prove an empty landscape, while modern practice still cannot date the first local herding.

Collaborative archaeology finds that reindeer riding has regionally varied origins and an uncertain growth history. The target may include later reindeer-herding homelands, but that does not prove every household rode or owned domestic reindeer in 1200. Wild reindeer use, transport, and herding are different questions.

Rivers crossing the polygon offered travel corridors and aquatic resources, while mountain and taiga routes demanded detailed seasonal judgment. The exact balance of fishing, hunting, gathering, exchange, and animal keeping remains locally undocumented. A broad label cannot choose supper for thousands of households.

sections.title: See families, companionship, children, and learning

items.text: Modern Baikal fieldwork describes gender distinctions as situational within an egalitarian Evenki social setting, rather than a rigid task chart. That finding challenges stereotypes but cannot be backdated eight centuries. Exact-period marriage, kinship, inheritance, adoption, and household membership remain undocumented for this entire target.

A Max Planck study describes companionship as a flexible yet durable basis of later Eastern Buryatia Evenki social organization. It offers a valuable comparison for cooperation and autonomy. It does not prove that thirteenth-century Aldan or Dzhugdzhur camps organized friendship, obligation, conflict, or leadership identically.

Children in later community research fish, observe herds, help treat animals, and train calves alongside adults. Participation can transmit routes, weather judgment, animal behavior, tools, and responsibilities. This is evidence for a living knowledge system, not an exact-period school timetable or universal childhood rule.

No classroom, textbook, or lesson plan is securely identified inside the polygon for 1200 to 1279. Children certainly learned speech, safety, food skills, social expectations, and local places. The teachers, ages, stories, games, discipline, and ceremonial learning remain unknown rather than available for cheerful invention.

UNESCO treats Indigenous environmental knowledge and language as integrated parts of living culture, developed with community contributors rather than extracted as anonymous facts. That principle matters here: oral transmission is evidence-bearing knowledge. The absence of medieval writing is not proof of silence, simplicity, or missing intelligence.

sections.title: Discuss health, healing, birth, and care honestly

items.text: Modern Northern Baikal ethnography documents knowledge of Gentiana algida and Rhodiola rosea as widely valued medicines, gathered through mobility and observation of animals. This is strong evidence for later Evenki healing practice. It is not proof of the same plants, doses, diagnoses, or meanings in 1200.

The medicine study connects prevention and treatment with resource scarcity and mobile hunting and herding. Carrying versatile remedies made practical sense in that later setting. Medieval residents also faced illness and injury, but no reviewed target source names their healer, remedy, dosage, surgical method, or diagnostic vocabulary.

Food plants in modern Evenki knowledge can cross boundaries between nourishment, medicine, ritual, and identity. Such categories need not match a modern pharmacy shelf. Still, the current study cannot be used to prescribe an exact-period recipe or claim that every community recognized the same plant authority.

A fourteenth- or fifteenth-century burial west of this target shows how bones may reveal age, strain, trauma, and pathology when preservation and context allow. It is later and culturally distinct, so it cannot diagnose target residents. It demonstrates method, not a borrowed patient record.

Pregnancy, birth, nursing, childhood illness, injury care, disability, aging, and grief were part of human life, yet the reviewed evidence does not identify exact target customs. Saying so protects families from fiction. Care certainly existed; who provided it, with what knowledge, and under which rules remains open.

sections.title: Ask about water, cleaning, waste, and toilets

items.text: The polygon follows major river and mountain-water systems, so water shaped travel, fishing, camp choice, drinking, cooking, and washing. Geometry cannot tell us whether a household boiled, filtered, stored, or carried water in a particular vessel. Those practices require features, residues, containers, or testimony.

Later portable-house studies show that camp organization responds to materials, weather, work, and movement. They do not document a standard medieval drain, sewer, bath, or wash station. A neat floor plan cannot be promoted into a sanitation system simply because modern readers would enjoy the plumbing diagram.

Mobile camps generate ash, food scraps, broken tools, animal waste, and human waste, but those materials preserve unevenly. Ethnoarchaeology helps explain that visibility problem. It does not authorize a universal disposal rule, nor does a sparse site prove that residents never cleaned their living area.

Toilet verdict: no reviewed source securely identifies a 1200 to 1279 latrine inside this exact polygon. People relieved themselves and managed the result, but the location, privacy rules, cleaning materials, seasonality, and disposal practices are unknown. No pipes is not the same as no hygiene.

Later ecological knowledge distinguishes insects, animals, water, weather, and seasonal tasks in fine detail. Such observation could support safe camp choices, yet it cannot fill a medieval sanitation blank. Respectful history labels the gap instead of inventing a tidy taiga bathroom with suspiciously modern house rules.

sections.title: Handle writing, art, and evidence without borrowing voices

items.text: No securely localized Tungusic-language text survives from 1200 to 1279 inside the exact polygon. This card therefore supplies no umbrella written sample. It does not borrow later Evenki or Even orthographies, Jurchen characters from southern sites, reconstructed proto-forms, Russian spellings, or modern community phrases.

The Arkhara inscription bears a date corresponding to 1 December 1127 and uses Jurchen writing. Arkhara lies south of the target and the object predates its interval. It is a valuable control showing why “known somewhere in a related language” is not “representative here.”

Jurchen's native-script materials make it the earliest written Tungusic language known to the cited linguistic study, although the evidence is limited. That achievement belongs to specific Jurchen contexts. It cannot be redistributed across every related language or pasted onto uninscribed northern camps.

Tangaralaakh rock imagery includes layers assigned broadly to the Neolithic, paleometal, Iron Age, and medieval periods, with some marks possibly refreshed later. The mixed chronology defeats an exact sample. A sign-like mark without secure date, language, and community is not a readable medieval sentence.

Oral knowledge is not a consolation prize for missing text. UNESCO's community-based work treats language and environmental knowledge as connected living systems. The historical problem is preservation and attribution: no recording from 1200 survives, so modern words must not be made to impersonate unnamed medieval speakers.

sections.title: Recognize achievements and end at an atlas seam

items.text: At 1279 the exact target vanishes. Olekminsk, Neryungri, Aldan, Bomnak, the central watershed, Ust-Maya, Dzhugdzhur, and Nelkan become Siberians, while Nikolaevsk becomes Yuan Dynasty. The map supplies no event explaining that split, so neither label is accepted as a historical successor.

The imported Siberians summary describes later Russian Siberiaks, making it especially unsafe for a 1279 continuity story. Yuan political history also cannot be stretched across every former probe. Neighboring summaries are discovery aids at best, not permission to overwrite unnamed local communities.

The 1279 owner pattern remains unchanged at the same probes in 1300 and 1400. Persistence proves only that the atlas reused its categories. It does not validate a sudden ethnic transformation, one conquest frontier, or an administrative reform reaching every river and mountain camp simultaneously.

Portable architecture, route memory, animal knowledge, fishing, hunting, plant use, teaching, care, and collaborative work were major achievements in later documented communities. Their exact medieval forms remain uncertain. Continuity honors local people and knowledge holders without turning any modern nation into the polygon's owner.

The safe ending is continuity with fell set to null, no predecessors, and no successors. The card ends because the exact id ends. That modest database decision avoids announcing a nonexistent collapse and leaves room for the many communities whose histories the broad label never adequately named.

ending.text: The exact tungusic-tribes feature ends at 1279 because the atlas repaints its northern East Siberian polygon, not because one people collapsed or disappeared. Eight sampled target locations become Siberians and Nikolaevsk becomes Yuan Dynasty, while the same owners persist at 1300 and 1400. The imported Siberians text concerns much later Russian Siberiaks, and the Yuan label cannot explain every former target community. No cited source identifies a single conquest, migration, language shift, successor state, or ceremony matching the software seam. Families, routes, ecological knowledge, social relationships, and distinct local histories continued. The override therefore uses fell set to null and names no predecessors or successors. Later Evenki, Even, Negidal, Sakha, and neighboring histories require community-specific research rather than inheritance from this retrospective umbrella.
